options.rationale: The figures do not measure the same thing, so the comparison cannot yet support any action. A shared definition shows whether a real gap exists and how large it is before anyone is retrained.

options.text: Support the retraining in the south, since a gap of 23 points between regions is too large to be explained by a difference in how jobs are counted.
options.rationale: The candidate assumes the size of the gap proves it is real. A 30-day window can catch far more repeat visits than a seven-day one, so nobody yet knows how much of the gap is performance.

options.text: Report the three figures with a footnote explaining the different counting rules, and let the operations director decide what to do about the south.
options.rationale: The candidate discloses the problem but leaves a misleading comparison as the basis for a decision. A footnote rarely changes how a headline figure is read, especially by someone who has already drawn a conclusion.

options.text: Ask the southern manager to adopt the seven-day rule used in the north so that her region's figure can be compared with the north directly.
options.rationale: This aligns two regions but picks one rule without agreeing which reflects the outcome that matters, and ignores the midlands, whose rule is unknown. The candidate standardises by convenience rather than by agreement.

questions.explanation: A quality metric is comparable only when everyone measures it the same way, which needs an operational definition: what is counted, over what period, by what rule. Before acting on differences between teams, sites or suppliers, check that the numbers describe the same thing. Otherwise corrective action is aimed at a measurement artefact, and any real performance gap stays unknown.
questions.mindset: Make sure a number means the same thing everywhere before comparing it.

questions.stem: Your team supports a travel company's booking site using Kanban. Over the past month the 'awaiting test' column has grown from three items to fourteen while 'in development' keeps filling. The team's single tester is working late, and lead time for small changes has doubled. Some developers say testing is not their job. There is no budget this quarter for another tester. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Agree a work-in-progress limit for the testing column with the team, so developers stop starting new items when it is full.
options.rationale: Work is being started faster than it can be finished. A limit makes the bottleneck visible on the board and stops new work piling up behind it, which is a change the team can make itself.

options.text: Ask developers to help clear the testing queue by pairing with the tester and adding automated checks to the items they build.
options.rationale: Quality is a whole-team responsibility, and spare capacity upstream is the fastest help the constrained step can get. Automated checks written by developers also reduce the testing load on future items.

options.text: Ask the resourcing manager to lend a tester from another product team until the queue is back under five items.
options.rationale: Borrowed capacity may clear today's queue, but the candidate treats a flow problem as a staffing one. With nothing else changed, the queue rebuilds as soon as the loan ends.

options.text: Group the waiting items into a weekly release so the tester can work through them in one batch with a single regression run.
options.rationale: Batching looks efficient for the tester, but the candidate lengthens lead time further, since every item now waits for the slowest one in its batch, and larger releases are harder to diagnose when they fail.

options.text: Let changes estimated at under a day go straight to release after code review, so the tester can focus on larger items.
options.rationale: Risk-based testing has its place, but here the candidate lowers the quality bar to match current capacity, without evidence that small changes are low-risk, rather than changing how the work flows.

questions.explanation: A growing queue in front of one step signals a flow problem, not only a staffing one: work is being started faster than it can be finished. Limiting work in progress exposes the bottleneck and stops new work piling up, and treating quality as a whole-team responsibility lets idle capacity upstream help the constrained step. Adding capacity, batching or skipping checks without changing the flow tends to move the queue rather than remove it.
questions.mindset: Stop starting and start finishing — quality belongs to the whole team, not one role.

questions.stem: Your project is building foundations for 30 wind turbines. The contract's sampling plan for anchor bolts says: from each lot of 2,000, inspect 80, and reject the lot if three or more fail the thread gauge. Today's lot had four failures. The supplier asks for a second sample of 80, arguing the first was unlucky, and proposes accepting the lot if that sample has two or fewer failures. Bolting is due to start on Monday. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Allow the second sample but judge the lot on all 160 bolts together, accepting it only if no more than six fail, which keeps the agreed rejection rate.
options.rationale: Doubling both sample and limit looks statistically fair. But the candidate rewrites the acceptance rule after seeing a failing result, and the combined rule carries a different risk from the one both parties agreed.

options.text: Reject the lot as the plan specifies, and ask the supplier to gauge every bolt in it at its own cost before resubmitting the lot for sampling.
options.rationale: The plan's protection depends on acting on the sample drawn. Re-sampling a failed lot until one passes raises the chance of accepting a bad lot, and supplier screening keeps the cost of the failure with the party that caused it.

options.text: Accept today's lot under tightened inspection, sampling the next three lots at double the size, so a genuine quality problem would show up quickly.
options.rationale: Tightened inspection after a failure is a real feature of sampling schemes, which makes this attractive. But it applies to future lots; it does not make a rejected lot acceptable, and these bolts go into concrete.

options.text: Have your own site team gauge all 2,000 bolts over the weekend, so the good ones can be used on Monday and the failures returned to the supplier.
options.rationale: This protects Monday and finds every bad bolt, so it is defensible. The candidate takes on appraisal cost and responsibility that belong to the supplier, and rewards the failed lot with free screening.

questions.explanation: An acceptance sampling plan is a pre-agreed balance of risk between buyer and seller, and it works only if the result of the sample is acted on. Drawing further samples from a failed lot until one passes, or rewriting the rule once a result is known, shifts that balance in the seller's favour. A rejected lot is handled through the remedies the plan or contract provides, such as screening, rework or replacement, with the cost resting where the failure arose.
questions.mindset: Act on the sample you agreed to take, not on the one you hope to draw next.

questions.stem: A digital bank's development team has listed three recurring problems from its retrospectives. Match each problem to the practice most likely to address it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Code from different developers is merged only on the last day of the sprint, and conflicts break features that worked in isolation.
Only one developer understands the interest-calculation module, and nobody else can review her changes effectively.
Developers write the code first and add tests afterwards, so the tests confirm what the code does rather than what it should do.

options.text: Continuous integration
options.rationale: Merging small changes to a shared branch many times a day, with an automated build and tests, surfaces conflicts within hours instead of on the last day of the sprint.

options.text: Pair programming
options.rationale: Working in pairs on the module spreads understanding of it and provides review as the code is written, which removes the single point of knowledge and of review.

options.text: Test-driven development
options.rationale: Writing the test before the code forces the expected behaviour to be stated first, so the test checks what the code should do rather than echoing what it happens to do.

options.text: A hardening sprint before each release
options.rationale: Not used. A hardening sprint moves testing and integration into a separate block at the end. It postpones all three problems rather than removing any of them, and lets defects live longer.

questions.explanation: Agile quality is built in through engineering practices that shorten the time between making a mistake and finding it. Frequent integration finds conflicts early, pairing spreads knowledge and reviews code as it is written, and writing tests first makes intended behaviour explicit. Deferring quality work to a dedicated phase at the end does the opposite, lengthening the feedback loop the practices are meant to shorten.
questions.mindset: Build quality in by shortening the time between a mistake and its discovery.

questions.stem: A research funder's hybrid programme has rebuilt its grant-application process in three stages. Last quarter, 96 per cent of applications passed eligibility checks first time, 90 per cent passed financial review first time and 98 per cent passed the panel paperwork check first time. Each stage manager reports a healthy figure. The funder handles 5,000 applications a quarter. Work out the figures below.

blanks.label: Percentage of applications that pass all three stages first time, to one decimal place
blanks.rationale: The stages are passed in sequence, so the first-time yields multiply: 0.96 × 0.90 × 0.98 = 0.8467, or 84.7 per cent. No single stage looks poor, yet roughly one application in six needs rework somewhere.

blanks.label: Number of applications a quarter that need rework at one or more stages, to the nearest whole number
blanks.rationale: Applications not passing every stage first time are 1 − 0.8467 = 0.1533 of the total: 5,000 × 0.1533 = 766.4, so about 766 applications a quarter.

blanks.label: Which stage, if brought to 100 per cent first time, would raise the overall figure most — eligibility, financial review or panel paperwork
blanks.rationale: Perfecting eligibility gives 0.90 × 0.98 = 88.2 per cent; perfecting financial review gives 0.96 × 0.98 = 94.1 per cent; perfecting panel paperwork gives 0.96 × 0.90 = 86.4 per cent. Financial review has the lowest yield, so it gains most.

questions.explanation: A process is only as good as the product of its stages: first-time yields multiply, so several stages that each look healthy can combine into a poor end-to-end result. Measuring the whole flow, rather than each stage in isolation, reveals how much rework the process really carries and shows which stage limits it. Improvement effort belongs where the lowest yield is, because that stage holds the whole figure down.
questions.mindset: Judge a process by its end-to-end yield, not by how good each stage looks on its own.

questions.stem: Your firm is repainting a steel railway bridge. The quality management plan, approved by the client's engineer as a contract document, requires paint-thickness readings at ten marked points on each girder. The site team has switched to an electronic gauge that logs thousands of readings per girder and finds thin spots the ten-point method missed. An internal audit has just recorded the switch as a nonconformance with the plan. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Submit a revision of the plan describing the electronic method to the client's engineer, and take the ten-point readings alongside it until approval is given.
options.rationale: The new method is better, but the plan is part of the contract and its approver is the client's engineer. Revising it through that route adopts the improvement properly, and keeping the agreed readings meanwhile means every girder still has the evidence the contract calls for.

options.text: Return to the ten-point method straight away, since the approved plan is the baseline, and record the electronic gauge as a lesson for future bridge contracts.
options.rationale: This restores compliance cleanly, which is why careful managers choose it. The candidate discards a method that is finding real defects and treats the plan as fixed rather than as a baseline with its own change route.

options.text: Close the audit finding as an observation, because the electronic method exceeds what the plan requires, and record the reasoning in the project's quality log.
options.rationale: Substance over form is appealing when the new method is plainly more thorough. But the contract sets the evidence the client will accept at handover, and only the client's engineer can agree that another method meets it.

options.text: Ask the firm's quality manager to update the plan to the electronic method and reissue it to the site team, so that plan and practice match once again.
options.rationale: Aligning plan and practice is the right instinct, and the quality manager owns the firm's quality system. The candidate overlooks that this plan was approved by the client as a contract document, so an internal reissue changes nothing the contract requires.

questions.explanation: When practice departs from an approved plan, the remedy depends on who approved the plan and what it is for, not only on which method is better. A plan that forms part of a contract can be changed only by the party that accepted it, and until it is changed the evidence it requires is still owed. Improvements should be brought into the baseline through its change route rather than abandoned or quietly adopted.
questions.mindset: Bring a better practice into the baseline through whoever owns the baseline.

questions.stem: Your team runs a university's online learning platform. The product owner consistently ranks new features above defect fixes, and 140 defects are now open, some more than a year old. She says new features win more course enrolments. Support staff tell you that three of the oldest defects generate around 200 help-desk tickets a month, but this has never been raised in backlog refinement. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree with the developers to reserve a fifth of each sprint's capacity for defect fixes, so the oldest defects are cleared without reopening the priority debate.
options.rationale: Reserving capacity for defects is a common practice, which makes this attractive. Agreed with the developers alone, it overrides the product owner's ordering of the backlog on information she has never seen.

options.text: Bring the ticket volumes and handling cost for the oldest defects to the next refinement, so the product owner can rank them against features on the same evidence.
options.rationale: The product owner owns the ordering, but she is ranking defects without knowing what they cost. Expressing that cost in the terms she uses for value lets defects compete fairly with features in every future decision.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to direct the product owner to fix every defect older than six months before any further features are taken into a sprint.
options.rationale: The candidate escalates before the product owner has been given the evidence, and replaces her judgement with a blanket rule that treats a trivial old defect the same as a costly one.

options.text: Plan a dedicated defect sprint next month, so the backlog is brought down in one concentrated push and feature work resumes straight afterwards.
options.rationale: A clean-up push feels decisive, but the candidate decides the product owner's priorities for her and changes nothing about the information she ranks with, so the backlog will grow again.

questions.explanation: Owning priority does not guarantee good prioritisation if the owner cannot see what quality failures cost. Defects compete fairly with features only when their cost — support load, lost users, workarounds — is expressed in the same terms used for value. The project manager's job is to put that evidence in front of the decision-maker, not to take the decision away from her.
questions.mindset: Show the decision-maker the cost of poor quality before questioning her decisions.

questions.stem: You are managing the fit-out of 400 cabins on a cruise ship. Two inspectors check veneer panels for finish defects. In a weekly comparison, they reached different pass or fail decisions on 30 per cent of the panels both had inspected, and the joinery subcontractor is disputing rejections. The specification says panels must be 'free of visible blemishes'. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Agree physical reference panels with the client that show the boundary between an acceptable and a rejectable finish.
options.rationale: 'Free of visible blemishes' leaves each inspector to supply their own standard. Boundary samples agreed with the client turn the words into a shared, checkable definition of acceptable.

options.text: Have both inspectors assess the same set of panels twice, without knowing which they have seen, to measure their consistency.
options.rationale: This tests whether each inspector agrees with themselves and with the other. Until the inspection itself is shown to be consistent, its results cannot settle disputes with the subcontractor.

options.text: Replace the inspector who rejects more panels, since the subcontractor's complaints suggest that standard is too strict.
options.rationale: The candidate assumes the stricter inspector is wrong. With no agreed standard, nobody knows which inspector is closer to what the client expects, and the disagreement would simply continue with someone new.

options.text: Ask the subcontractor to rework every disputed panel, so only panels that both inspectors would pass go into the cabins.
options.rationale: This protects the client but treats inconsistent inspection as a product defect. The candidate pays for rework the specification may not require and leaves the measurement problem in place.

options.text: Have both inspectors check every panel, so that each pass or fail decision is confirmed by a second person before it stands.
options.rationale: Double inspection sounds rigorous, but two inconsistent judgements do not make a reliable one. The candidate doubles appraisal cost and multiplies the disagreements without fixing their cause.

questions.explanation: Before inspection results are used to judge a product, check that the measurement itself can be trusted. Frequent disagreement between inspectors usually stems from an undefined standard or an inconsistent measurement process, and the remedies are a shared operational definition — often physical boundary samples — and a check of how repeatable and reproducible the inspectors' decisions are. Adding inspection on top of an unreliable measurement multiplies the disagreement.
questions.mindset: Check that the measurement is trustworthy before trusting what it says about the product.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme is commissioning a new bread line: equipment is installed to a fixed plan and its control software is tuned in sprints. A control chart tracks the average weight of each hourly sample of loaves, and every point so far lies within the control limits. Each box describes one stretch of the chart. Select the stretch that most warrants investigation for a special cause.

graphic.title: Loaf-weight control chart divided into five stretches of hourly samples
graphic.caption: Select a stretch. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between stretches, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Hours 1–8: points scattered either side of the centre line, none near a limit
regions.rationale: Random scatter about the centre line, well inside the limits, is what a stable process looks like. There is nothing here to investigate.

regions.label: Hours 9–16: eight consecutive points above the centre line, all inside the limits
regions.rationale: Eight points in a row on one side of the centre line is very unlikely by chance even though none breaches a limit. A run like this suggests the process mean has shifted, for example a change in dough mix or oven setting, and calls for investigation.

regions.label: Hour 17: one point close to, but inside, the upper control limit
regions.rationale: A single point near a limit is eye-catching, which is why it is chosen. Occasional points near the limits are expected in a stable process; on its own, one point inside the limits is not a signal.

regions.label: Hours 18–24: points either side of the centre line, slightly more spread than hours 1–8
regions.rationale: A little more spread over a few hours, still well within the limits and centred, is within normal variation. Reading it as a change confuses ordinary fluctuation with a pattern.

regions.label: Hour 25: one point just below the centre line, taken just after the flour hopper was refilled
regions.rationale: A known event beside a point invites a causal story, but the point itself is unremarkable. Investigating it because of the coincidence treats noise as a signal.

questions.explanation: A process can be out of control while every point is within the control limits. Non-random patterns — such as seven or more consecutive points on one side of the centre line — signal that something in the process has changed, even though no single point is extreme. Reading a control chart means looking for patterns as well as breaches, and leaving isolated, unremarkable points alone.
questions.mindset: Look for patterns on a control chart, not only for points outside the lines.
